name: Greet an unfamiliar dog safely
blurb: Most dog bites happen during greetings that the dog never consented to. The correct approach is quick to learn and worth teaching every child you know.
steps: Ask the owner first, every time, and accept no as an answer without negotiating.
Let the dog choose: stand side-on, avoid direct eye contact, and let it come to you rather than reaching towards it.
Do not loom over the dog or reach over its head — approach low and to the side of the neck or chest if it invites contact.
Do the three-second rule: stroke briefly, stop, and see whether the dog asks for more or moves away.
Learn to recognise a dog that is tolerating rather than enjoying contact, and stop.
Teach children the same routine, and never let them hug or lean over an unfamiliar dog.
tips: A dog behind a fence, in a car, on a lead beside its owner, or eating is not available for greeting.
Yellow lead or bandana schemes often mean "give me space". Respect them.
proof: You can run the whole greeting routine naturally and explain it to a child.
